title: Cache-Aside
subtitle: Lazy-loading cache patterns, read/write flows, solving concurrency races, and negative caching guards.
keyTakeaways: In Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading), application code coordinates both the cache and the database: checking cache first, reading DB on a miss, and populating the cache.
On database updates, the application should DELETE (invalidate) the cache key rather than updating it, avoiding out-of-order write races under concurrent requests.
Defend against cache penetration (repeated queries for non-existent IDs) by storing a null sentinel with a short TTL (negative caching) or deploying a Bloom filter.
architectureDiagram:
CACHE-ASIDE READ & WRITE FLOW
READ PATH (Cache Miss):                      WRITE PATH (Invalidate on Write):
  [App Server] -- 1. GET key --> [Redis]       [App Server] -- 1. UPDATE row -> [Database]
       |         (Miss: nil)                     |                              |
       +--------- 2. SELECT ---> [Database]      +------------ 2. DEL key ----> [Redis]
       |         (Returns row)                   (Next read will lazy-load fresh value)
       +--------- 3. SETEX ----> [Redis]

sections.heading: Why Delete-on-Write Beats Update-on-Write
sections.body: A frequent architectural mistake in Cache-Aside is having the application update the cache with new data after writing to the database. If Request A and Request B update the same row concurrently, Request A writes to the database first and Request B writes second. But if Request B's cache write completes first and Request A's arrives second due to network jitter, the cache is permanently corrupted with Request A's stale data until TTL expiration. Deleting the cache key (`DEL`) forces the next reader to fetch authoritative state from the database.
bullets: Lazy Population: Caches only the active working set; cold records never consume expensive RAM.

The Read/Write Race Window: A theoretical race exists where a concurrent reader reads the old DB value during a miss, a writer updates the DB and deletes the cache, and then the reader sets the stale value into Redis. In practice, DB updates take longer than cache sets, making this rare. Using Redis `SET ... NX` or Memcached leases eliminates this edge case.
Cold Start Headroom: A freshly deployed or flushed cache cluster experiences a 100% miss rate; warm critical static datasets proactively before directing production traffic.

sections.heading: Guarding Against Cache Penetration and Stampedes
sections.body: If malicious actors or crawler bugs repeatedly query IDs that do not exist (e.g., negative integers or random UUIDs), every request misses the cache and hits the primary database directly, known as Cache Penetration. Production systems defend against this using two primary techniques.
bullets: Negative Caching: When the database returns zero rows, write a sentinel value (`__NULL__`) into Redis with a short TTL (30 to 60 seconds). Subsequent requests for the non-existent entity return null directly from memory.
Bloom Filter Guard: Maintain a compact in-memory Bloom filter of all valid entity IDs; drop requests for keys not present in the filter before querying either Redis or the database.
Schema Key Versioning: Prefix all cache keys with a schema version (`user:profile:v2:{id}`) so deployments introducing breaking serialization changes bypass old cached records cleanly.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple mental model; only actively requested data occupies memory; decoupled from database storage engine internals.
tradeOffs.cons: Initial read incurs a three-hop latency penalty (Cache miss -> DB query -> Cache write); requires application code orchestration.
tradeOffs.bestFor: General-purpose read-heavy web APIs, user profile data, product catalogs, and content management systems.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero cache miss latency penalty for users; delivers predictable p99 read latencies from the moment traffic shifts.
tradeOffs.cons: Consumes memory caching entities that may never be read; requires dedicated background data replication pipelines.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Featured homepage banners, active system configuration flags, and viral social media posts.

interviewTip: In interviews, explicitly state why you delete the cache on write rather than updating it: 'On write, we update the database first and issue a DEL to Redis. Updating Redis directly introduces race conditions where out-of-order network packets can permanently poison the cache with stale data.'
